subsubtopic: EARTHQUAKE IN MEXICO-NEED FOR AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada want to extend not only sympathy but also practical help to the people of Mexico following the devastation caused by yesterday's earthquake. The Mexican people and Government face massive problems. Direct victims of the quake need medical treatment. Emergency water and sewage facilities must be provided to prevent epidemic disease. Housing must be provided for people whose homes have been destroyed. There must be emergency distribution of food.
In the name of humanity, the Government of Canada must move quickly to help. Working in co-operation with recognized relief agencies, our Government should announce an immediate program to match, dollar for dollar, all private contributions. Direct Government-to-Government aid should also be given to help repair communication and transportation links, as well as water and sewage lines.
Canada should make the strongest possible representation to the International Monetary Fund to reverse yesterday's badly timed decision that cancelled $450 million worth of loans to Mexico. I urge the Canadian Government to announce immediate plans for a comprehensive and generous program to help the people of Mexico.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S ACHIEVEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government can count on the co-operation of several groups in its efforts to improve the lives of Canadians, Quebecers and the people of Beauce whom I have the honour to represent.
Since we came to power, our Government has been listening to the people, and to confirm the truth of this statement, I can mention that 67 per cent of Quebec business people say they are satisfied with the way the Mulroney Government is running the country. Business people across this country are our main partners in creating jobs.

September 20, 1985
The newspaper Les Affaires of August 31 published a detailed report on how business people feel about the present Government, and it was a very positive analysis.
Also, now that the Macdonald Report has been tabled, Canadian citizens will be able to consider their national future in its broadest terms, now that the Commission has described with great frankness and energy the choices open to Canadians.
This is a golden opportunity for elected representatives to change the face of this country and to redefine its social, industrial and even national frontiers. The new trade agreements with our neighbour to the South, the restructuring of social programs and Quebec's place in Canada are subjects that deserve serious, frank and thorough reflection.
Canada's future depends on its ability to react quickly to change, and the survival of this country will depend on that ability.

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF HERRING FISHERY IN GLOUCESTER RIDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last two weeks have been highlighted by mementous events within the herring fishing industry in the constituency of Gloucester. The future of the industry is threatened.
During that time I had an opportunity to meet with officials of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans as well as spokesmen for producers, plant workers and fishermen from my riding.
The current crisis in the Gulf of St. Lawrence stems from the disagreement between fishermen and Department of Fisheries and Oceans biologists.
The quotas established last year were expected to cover a three-month fishing season, but it actually took fewer than eight days to fill them.
If coastal fishermen can catch 8,000 metric tons within eight days, should we question the accuracy of the data provided by the biologists?
We learn from fishermen with over 20 years of experience that this year herring stocks are abundant enough to allow for double the established quota.
In the interest of people whose sole source of income is fishing, I would urge the Minister to reconsider his decision not to raise quotas. The full impact of this situation will be felt not only by the fishermen who will be unable to sell their fish next year, but also by the producers who will already have lost their markets.
I would be remiss to conclude without emphasizing that we would be making a mistake by ignoring the representations of
my constituents. Therefore I ask the Minister to review the data and give those fishermen a fighting chance to earn their living.

Mr. Speaker, I urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to dissociate himself altogether from the Environment Canada Report dealing with the impact on farm lands of the municipal drainage outlet program established under the Canada-Ontario subsidiary agreement for Eastern Ontario and said to be a preliminary evaluation.

This report is a direct attack on the farmers of eastern Ontario who requested funding, and on all the minicipalities which administered these funds. It would seem that the authors of the report had made up their minds on the conclusions before they even started. Eastern Ontario farmers do not agree with these findings and I doubt if any of them were even consulted.
Eastern Ontario has always lagged behind other areas of the province, and programs such as the one I just described have assisted in upgrading the land. More funding is needed to allow the farmers of our part of the country to be more competitive with others.
I call upon my colleagues, the Member for Stormont-Dun-das (Mr. Warner), the Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt), the Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), the Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper), the Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) and others to join me in condemning this report.

subsubtopic: HIGH CHEMICAL INPUT COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share excerpts from a letter concerning drought assistance written to me by a farm couple in the Cabri area of southwestern Saskatchewan. They say:
It angers us to hear about how Government plans to write down debts with farm credit. There are farmers in this area, and I am sure in other areas, that are in financial difficulty because they had to have land at outrageously high prices. They never stop to think there may come a time when there would be no crop or when the price drops or when there is no market for our grain. That's all happened before.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, they ask why should the foolhardy be rewarded with a loan writedown while the prudent get to foot the bill? Why should the guy who outbid everybody else at a land auction now be bailed out by those whom he outbid?
The letter continues:
If you want to help us in a positive manner and help all farmers, try to reduce our input costs. I think the cost of chemical is a big rip-off and these companies should be investigated. I think most all farmers spend a good portion of their income on grasshopper poison in the drought area, and maybe Governments could pay for that if they want to help.
This letter is fairly representative and contains some good, sound advice. I recommend these useful and practical suggestions to the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), Chairman of the Task Force on Drought, and to the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise).

A Minister of the Crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a despatch or other state paper not before the House, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the Table.

To be cited, a document must be quoted or specifically used to influence debate.
I also appreciate that there have times in the past when the very narrow definition of "debate" has been used to defeat a request such as the one I am making. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think we should extend to the people and the Government of Mexico our sincere sympathy after this terrible disaster.
September 20, 1985

The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) met with the Mexican Ambassador last night to offer him our condolences and to inform him of the measures the Government of Canada has now taken to provide assistance.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has two concerns.
First, regarding the victims in Mexico: we want to help them, and that is why last night I announced that the Canadian International Development Agency was making $1 million available to organizations experienced in relief work. We expect to receive specific requests from these organizations within the next few hours, as soon as requirements have been specified. A CIDA expert on emergency relief has left for Mexico and she will be reporting to us on the situation.
Second, regarding thousands of Canadians who are worried about close relatives or friends in Mexico and whom we want to reassure as soon as possible.
Emergency procedures provided for this type of disaster are now in effect. As of yesterday afternoon, the Operations Centre at the Department of External Affairs is on a 24-hour schedule. The Centre's telephone number has been announced by the media, and I will repeat it here: area code 613-996-8885.
People who are worried about Canadians in Mexico can call the Centre and leave the names of the persons about whom they want to obtain information.
A team of six consular officers from the Department of External Affairs left Canada at 10:30 this morning to go and assist our embassy staff. They will be responsible for helping all Canadians who need assistance. The officers are fluent in Spanish and know Mexico very well. As information becomes available, it will be transmitted to the relatives and friends in Canada who contacted us.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: EARTHQUAKE IN MEXICO-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I rise to express shock and concern at the news of the tragic earthquake disaster in Mexico. I also want to express sympathy to the people of Mexico and, in particular, to all those who lost loved ones because of this disaster.
At least since 1981, when the President of Mexico paid an official visit to our country, we have had a special relationship with Mexico, a relationship involving growing closeness in many ways. Therefore, news of a disaster, like the earthquake that struck Mexico yesterday, comes as a matter of special concern to Canadians both in human terms and because of that deep and wide special relationship.
We are pleased to hear of the emergency measures announced by the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Vezina). I would like to ask the Minister whether the Government could give serious consideration to increasing the special aid fund which she announced yesterday. The news of the
Statements by Ministers
extent of the damage created by the earthquake indicates that it is of catastrophic proportions. Certainly the Government should be looking at the matter of urgency, as to what more we could do, not only by providing funds but by providing such things as mobile homes, medical supplies, communications equipment, and technical experts in a whole host of areas not just medical doctors but also engineering and construction people.
Second, it is necessary for the Government to confirm that it is doing everything possible to assist Canadians who may be stranded in Mexico because of the earthquake. It may well be necessary for special evacuation measures to be taken, possibly involving planes of the Canadian Armed Forces, as well as special communications networks in addition to what the Minister has announced.
To conclude, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I want to express our shock and concern at the extent of the tragedy connected with the catastrophic earthquake that struck Mexico yesterday, as well as to express our deepest sympathy to the people of Mexico, in particular to those who lost members of their family, friends and relatives in this earthquake.

We wish to extend our heartfelt condolences to the people of Mexico and assure them that the Canadian Government will make a sizeable financial contribution to help them through this emergency.

subsubtopic: EARTHQUAKE IN MEXICO-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister's statement must be regarded as nothing more than a preliminary expression of sympathy for the disaster that has overtaken the people of Mexico. As 1 said in my statement under the provisions of Standing Order 22 this morning, the people of Canada want to extend practical help and not just sympathy.
One million dollars from CIDA to help NGOs with their relief activities cannot, in any way, be regarded as a considered response from Canada to Mexico in this time of tragedy. The earthquake has done billions of dollars of damage to Mexico. Buildings have been destroyed. Transportation and communication links have been disrupted. As the Minister knows, following any earthquake there are problems with sanitation and disease. These problems will be much greater in Mexico City with a population of 18 million people. Considering this devastation, unless today's announcement is followed quickly, and I stress the word "quickly", by the annoucement of a much more comprehensive program, the $1 million will be an insult to the people of Mexico in this time of tragedy.
A more comprehensive program would include at least two components. The first would be a matching dollar for dollar program with recognized relief agencies. Many Canadians will want to make direct contributions to an aid program, and our Government should encourage it by matching dollar for dollar.

September 20, 1985

The second would be a program of direct Government to Government aid to help Mexico rebuild infrastructure which has been destroyed by the earthquake. This kind of aid would include equipment, expertise and financial help.
In addition, our aid proposals should not be considered in isolation from other events affecting Mexico. It is offensive in the extreme that on the very day when Mexico was hit by the devastation of an earthquake, the Internaitonal Monetary Fund suspended $450 million of loans to that country. This action symbolizes the insensitivity of the IMF to the suffering of people in many countries where it has cracked the whip and withdrawn loans from Governments desperately trying to meet the needs of their people. If the Canadian Government is truly concerned about the tragedy facing the Mexican people, it will use all the power and prestige it has with the IMF to reverse that decision and to restore the loan.
The close ties between Canada and Mexico are shown by the fact that there may be as many as 35,000 Canadians in that country now. The Government has taken steps to establish contact. I commend it for that, but I urge it to bring in a much more comprehensive program to begin to address the needs of the people of Mexico.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 NORTHLAND BANK SITUATION

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 31 NORTHLAND BANK SITUATION
speechtext:
I am sorry if there was some confusion. As I understand the Standing Orders, they contemplate motions under Standing Order 31 at this time and on two days a week after Questions on the Order Paper. I can assure the Hon. Member that I would know it if I did not have a crib sheet.
The Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) sent me notice of his intent to seek leave to move a motion under Standing Order 31. As he knows, in considering an application for an emergency debate under that Standing Order, the Chair must judge whether it meets the strict criteria required. In the letter which I received from the Hon. Member, certain matters were raised. I must say to him that the holding of a press conference and the allegations made by the President of the Northland Bank are not of themselves sufficient to constitute a genuine emergency as contemplated by the Standing Order. Neither, I should remind Hon. Members, has the action or inaction of a Minister ever been accepted as a justification for granting an emergency debate. It is only the emergency itself,
September 20, 1985

if its existence is accepted, which can constitute grounds for debate.
Our precedents clearly indicate that the imminent, potential collapse or failure of a bank-and in this case it would be the second-and its repercussions for the banking industry as a whole has and does constitute, in my view, a genuine emergency as envisioned by the Standing Order. The Chair must then consider whether an early opportunity of debating the matter is likely to be available. As Hon. Members well know, there is a Government notice of motion on the Notice Paper but, as yet, the Chair has no clear indication of when that motion is likely to come up for debate. However, I am advised that conversations continue as to whether there will be a debate.
While I find that the emergency questions have been met, today I am not satisfied, as yet, that there is a sufficiently urgent need to change today's Order Paper to have that matter debated today.
